steps.body: Triangles get **two family systems at once**. By **sides**: scalene (no equal sides), isosceles (at least two equal — that's our definition), equilateral (all three equal). By **angles**: acute (all under 90°), right (one exactly 90°), obtuse (one over 90°). Every triangle earns one label from EACH system.

widget.prompt: A triangle has sides 5, 5, and 8. Which side-family is it in?

choices.label: Isosceles
choices.feedback: Right — the pair of 5s makes it isosceles (at least two equal sides).
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens classify the triangle as isosceles.

choices.label: Equilateral
choices.feedback: Equilateral needs ALL THREE sides equal — the 8 breaks that. Two equal sides makes isosceles.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the equilateral claim.

choices.label: Scalene
choices.feedback: Scalene means NO equal sides, but 5 and 5 match. That pair makes it isosceles.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the scalene claim.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the pair of 5s makes it isosceles (at least two equal sides).

explanationVariants: The 5-5 pair puts it in isosceles.
At least two equal sides is all isosceles asks.

widget.prompt: A triangle has angles 90°, 45°, 45°. Which angle-family is it in?

choices.label: Right
choices.feedback: Right — one angle is exactly 90°. (Its equal 45s also make it isosceles — one label from each system.)
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens classify the triangle as right.

choices.label: Acute
choices.feedback: Acute needs ALL angles under 90°, and one is exactly 90°. That single square corner makes it a right triangle.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the acute claim.

choices.label: Obtuse
choices.feedback: Obtuse needs an angle OVER 90°. The biggest here is exactly 90°, which is the right-triangle mark.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the obtuse claim.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — one angle is exactly 90°. (Its equal 45s also make it isosceles — one label from each system.)

hints: Is it under, exactly, or over 90°?

steps.body: The systems **combine**: that 90-45-45 triangle is a **right isosceles** triangle — one label from each system, worn together. And since equilateral means all three sides equal, every equilateral triangle is automatically **isosceles** too (three equal sides certainly contains two). One more tool: a triangle's angles always add to **180°**.

explanationVariants: Three equal angles adding to 180° must each be 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

widget.prompt: An equilateral triangle's three angles are all equal and add to 180°. How many degrees is each angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 90° would make it a right angle — but 3 × 90 = 270, too much for a triangle. Equal shares of 180 are 60° each.
120 divides 360 by 3 — that's a full turn, not a triangle's angle sum. Use 180: 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

widget.prompt: Can a triangle be RIGHT and EQUILATERAL at the same time?
widget.blocker: Three 60° angles cannot include a 90° angle.

choices.label: No — three 60° angles rule it out
choices.feedback: Right — every equilateral angle is exactly 60°, so a 90° corner can never appear.
choices.evidenceText: Three 60° angles cannot include a 90° angle.

choices.label: Yes — equal sides make it work
choices.feedback: Equal sides force all three angles to 60°, and 60 ≠ 90. The side condition itself blocks the right angle.
choices.evidenceText: The always claim fails the required blocker test.

choices.label: Yes — right angles force equal sides
choices.feedback: A right triangle's angles are 90 plus two others — they can't all be 60°, so a right triangle is never equilateral.
choices.evidenceText: The always-reverse claim fails the required blocker test.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — every equilateral angle is exactly 60°, so a 90° corner can never appear.

hints: What are an equilateral triangle's angles?
explanationVariants: The two labels demand incompatible angles.
Three equal sides includes two equal sides.

widget.prompt: A triangle has sides 7, 7, 7. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: It is both equilateral and isosceles
choices.feedback: Right — all three equal makes it equilateral, and having (at least) two equal makes it isosceles too.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens classify the triangle as equilateral and isosceles.

choices.label: It is equilateral but NOT isosceles
choices.feedback: That treats isosceles as EXACTLY two equal sides. Our definition is at least two — so equilateral triangles qualify automatically.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the equilateral claim.

choices.label: It is scalene
choices.feedback: Scalene means no equal sides — but all three here are 7. This triangle sits at the top of the equal-sides ladder.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the scalene claim.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — all three equal makes it equilateral, and having (at least) two equal makes it isosceles too.

hints: Our isosceles rule: at least two equal.
Does 7, 7, 7 have at least two equal?
Take the systems one at a time.
explanationVariants: The 90° makes it right; the all-different sides make it scalene: right scalene.
Angle system says right (one 90°); side system says scalene (no equal pair).

widget.prompt: A triangle has angles 30°, 60°, 90°, and all three sides are different lengths. Which pair of labels fits it?

choices.label: Right scalene
choices.feedback: Right — the 90° angle gives right, and three different sides give scalene.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens classify the triangle as right and scalene.

choices.label: Right isosceles
choices.feedback: The angle label is correct, but isosceles needs at least two equal sides — this one has none. Side system says scalene.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the right and isosceles claim.

choices.label: Obtuse scalene
choices.feedback: The side label is correct, but obtuse needs an angle OVER 90° — the biggest here is exactly 90°, which means right.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the obtuse and scalene claim.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Use the family path, fixed triangle givens, or the required example, counterexample, or blocker evidence.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the 90° angle gives right, and three different sides give scalene.

takeaways: Sides: scalene / isosceles (at least two equal) / equilateral; angles: acute / right / obtuse.
Every triangle wears one label from each system — like right isosceles.
Equilateral is always isosceles, and never right: its angles are locked at 60°.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Count the equal sides.** None equal → scalene. At least two equal → isosceles. All three equal → equilateral (which still counts as isosceles). The angle labels are a separate question — sides first.

explanationVariants: Two equal sides is the isosceles test, and 4 = 4.

widget.prompt: A triangle has sides 4, 6, 4. Which side-family is it in?

choices.label: Isosceles
choices.feedback: Right — the two 4s make at least one equal pair.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens classify the triangle as isosceles.

choices.label: Scalene
choices.feedback: Scalene means no equal sides, but 4 and 4 match. One pair is enough for isosceles.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the scalene claim.

choices.label: Equilateral
choices.feedback: Equilateral needs all three equal — the 6 breaks that. The 4-4 pair makes it isosceles.
choices.evidenceText: The fixed givens contradict the equilateral claim.
